title: Orders above the customer's own average (correlated subquery)
problem_md:
Customer success wants to spot *unusually large* orders: orders whose value is higher than **that same customer's
average order value**. Guest orders (`customer_id IS NULL`) have no customer and must be ignored.

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  INTEGER,          -- NULL = guest checkout
  order_date   TEXT NOT NULL,
  total_amount REAL NOT NULL
);
```

> Money columns are `REAL` in this sandbox (they would be `NUMERIC(12,2)` in production PostgreSQL). Dates are ISO `'YYYY-MM-DD'` text.

**Task.** Return `order_id`, `customer_id`, `total_amount`, `customer_avg` (the customer's average
`total_amount` across all of their orders, rounded to 2 decimals) for orders **strictly greater** than that
average. Order by `order_id`.

examples.explanation: Order 8 equals the average, so it is not strictly greater. Customer 2 has a single order, which can never exceed its own average.

hints: For each outer row you need an aggregate over *other rows of the same customer* - a subquery that references the outer query.
`WHERE o.total_amount > (SELECT AVG(i.total_amount) FROM orders i WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id)`.
Use the same correlated subquery (wrapped in ROUND) in the SELECT list for `customer_avg`. Guest rows drop out on their own: `i.customer_id = NULL` is never true.
starter_code:
-- Write your query here
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
solution_code:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.customer_id,
       o.total_amount,
       ROUND((SELECT AVG(i.total_amount)
              FROM orders i
              WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id), 2) AS customer_avg
FROM orders o
WHERE o.total_amount > (SELECT AVG(i.total_amount)
                        FROM orders i
                        WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id)
ORDER BY o.order_id;
solution_md:
**Correlated subquery.** The inner `SELECT AVG(...) ... WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id` references the outer
row, so it is (logically) re-evaluated for every order. It is also a *scalar* subquery - it returns exactly one
value - which is why it can sit in both `SELECT` and `WHERE`.

- Customer 1's average is (1000 + 2000 + 3000 + 1500) / 4 = 1875, so orders 2 and 3 qualify.
- Order 8 (250) equals customer 4's average: `>` excludes it.
- Guest order 10: `i.customer_id = NULL` is UNKNOWN for every row, the subquery's `AVG` is NULL, and
  `5000 > NULL` is not true - so it disappears without any explicit filter. (Being explicit with
  `AND o.customer_id IS NOT NULL` is still good for readability.)

**Window-function alternative** (one pass, usually faster on large tables, no repeated subquery):

```sql
SELECT order_id, customer_id, total_amount, ROUND(customer_avg, 2) AS customer_avg
FROM (
  SELECT o.*, AVG(total_amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_avg
  FROM orders o
  WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
) t
WHERE total_amount > customer_avg
ORDER BY order_id;
```

Note you cannot reference a window function in `WHERE` directly - hence the derived table/CTE.

**Performance.** PostgreSQL may execute the correlated version as a nested loop calling the subplan per row;
an index on `orders (customer_id)` (ideally `INCLUDE (total_amount)` for index-only scans) keeps each probe cheap.
For big tables the window or a pre-aggregated CTE (`GROUP BY customer_id` joined back) is the safer choice.
